extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, typesetters, and printers
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed typographic and copyediting rules for hyphenation, word division, footnotes, indexing, tables, spacing, indentation, and technical terms used in book and journal production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en-dash in capitals or multiword components
rubrics_metrics.description: Where such words are set in capitals (e.g., in headlines), or where one of the components contains more than one word, an en-dash should be used in place of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago freight traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate with adverbs ending in -ly or when following noun/qualifying predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect by a hyphen adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in "-ly"; nor such combinations when following the noun, or qualifying a predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: highly developed species; a man well known in the neighborhood; do not hyphenate in "Her gown and carriage were strictly up to date."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate, as a rule, nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other — that is, one component derived from a transitive verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, fool-killer, office-holder, well-wisher, property-owner; hero-worship, child-study; wood-turning, clay-modeling. Exceptions: common/brief compounds like lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader, bookkeeper, stockholder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate present-participle + noun forming new noun or absolute participial constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united (1) with a noun to form a new noun with a meaning different from that conveyed by the two words separately, (2) with a preposition used absolutely (i.e., not governing a following noun), to form a noun, should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, working-man; "the putting-in or taking-out of a hyphen."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work by syllable-count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "book", "house", "mill", "room", "shop", and "work" should be printed as one compact word without a hyphen when the prefixed noun contains only one syllable; hyphenated when it contains two; printed as two separate words when it contains three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook, notebook; pocket-book, story-book; reference book. boathouse, clubhouse; engine-house, power-house; commill, handmill, sawmill; water-mill, paper-mill; bedroom, classroom; tinshop, workshop; handwork, woodwork. Exceptions: rare combinations or for appearance's sake (source-book, wheat-mill, school work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate occupation compounds (maker/dealer) and multiple-occupation nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "maker," "dealer," and other words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman, the poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions: a few short everyday words like bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rule for 'store' compounds by syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "store" should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'fellow' always hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "fellow" are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds of family/relation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "father," "mother," "brother," "sister," "daughter," "parent," and "foster" should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, sister-nation, foster-son, daughter-cells, parent-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'great-' for fourth-degree descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "great," indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds with 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "life" and "world" require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'skin' by syllable-count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "skin" with words of one syllable are to be printed as one word; with words of more than one, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds of 'master'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "master" should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke. Exception: masterpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'god' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "god" are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate fractions' numerator-denominator when spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers, spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "two-thirds", "four and five-sevenths", "thirty-hundredths"; but do not hyphenate in constructs like "one half of his fortune..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate combinations with 'half', 'quarter', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Half," "quarter," etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, half-year, half-title, quarter-mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes semi/demi/bi/tri generally no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: "Semi," "demi," "bi," "tri," etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, biweekly, bipartisan, trimonthly. Exceptions: long or unusual formations such as semi-centennial, demi-relievo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'self-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "self" are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' depend on number syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with "fold" are to be printed as one word if the number contains only one syllable; if it contains more, as two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with suffix 'like' by syllable and proper-noun rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by the suffixation of "like" to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable (except when ending in /); if it contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate titles with vice/ex/elect/general/lieutenant elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vice," "ex," "elect," "general," and "lieutenant," constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'by-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "by-" should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate CO-, pre-, re- when followed by same vowel; otherwise usually no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes "co-", "pre-", and "re-", when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, take a hyphen; but, as a rule, they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstal. Exceptions: with proper names, long or unusual formations, or where omission changes meaning (pre-Raphaelite, re-cover vs recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit hyphen from today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint/standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen from "today," "tomorrow," "tonight," "viewpoint," "standpoint."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: (See 119.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles un-/in-/a- usually no hyphen; non- usually hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles "un-," "in-," and "a-" do not usually require a hyphen. The particle "non-" ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate; non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious; but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'quasi-' prefixed words
rubrics_metrics.description: "Quasi" prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate 'over'/'under' prefixes except rare cases
rubrics_metrics.description: "Over" and "under" prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy words, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, underfed; but: over-soul, under-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin preposition prefixes (ante/anti/inter/intra/post/sub/super) usually no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The Latin prepositions "ante," "anti," "inter," "intra," "post," "sub," and "super" prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antidote, antiseptic (but: anti-imperialistic), international, interstate, intramural (but: intra-atomic), postgraduate, subtitle, subconscious. Exceptions: ante-bellum, anti-Semitic, inter-university.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate extra/infra/supra/ultra as a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: "Extra," "infra," "supra," and "ultra" as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of compound words occurring together with common element omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of two or more compound words occurring together, which have one of their component elements in common, this element is frequently omitted from all but the last word, and its implication should be indicated by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces. Note: some regard this hyphen as objectionable Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate prefix/suffix as particle or incomplete syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "The prefix a-"; "The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -kin."

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of everyday words to be hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of words of everyday occurrence which should be hyphenated and do not fall under previous classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: after-years, bas-relief, birth-rate, blood-feud, common-sense, cross-examine, cross-reference, cross-section, page-proof, death-rate, pay-roll, feast-day, post-office, fountain-head, well-being, guinea-pig, son-in-law, horse-power, subject-matter, will-power, man-of-war, thought-process, title-page, wave-length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions; carry whole word to next line where spacing allows
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words. Wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle (215).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide two-letter syllables in wide measures; limit divisions of short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide or a syllable of two letters, if possible to avoid it. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid dividing 'only' as on-ly; rare division for 'office' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive hyphenated line endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen, if at all avoidable. The next-to-last line in a paragraph ought not to end in a divided word; the last line should contain at least four letters in measures of 15 ems and up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid a broken word at the bottom of a recto page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or separate initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary. Do not separate the initials of a name, or such combinations as a.d., P.M., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional marks with the section they precede
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) in the middle of a sentence from the section which it precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the mark over with the matter to which it pertains (220).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide words according to pronunciation (American), not derivation (English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide according to pronunciation (the American system), not according to derivation (the English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); knowledge -> knowl-edge (not demo-).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on etymological lines when compatible with pronunciation and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: However, divide on etymological lines, or according to derivation and meaning, as far as compatible with pronunciation and good spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dis-pleasure preferred to displeas-nre; avoid monstrosities like Passo-ver, diso-bedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid terminating line in soft c, g, or in -ing split; carry -ing to next line
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or g, or in a / (sound). If impossible, divide pro-cess, not proc-ess; necessary -> ne-cessary; in present participles carry -ing into next line (spa-cing not spac-ing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule differs from some dictionaries (e.g., Webster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel where practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. If a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel over to next line (read-able, convert-ible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); particu-lar (not partic-ular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives when dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid additional hyphens in divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson, not object-lesson; fellow-being, not jellow-being; poverty-stricken, not pov-erty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as one letter in division decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; therefore do not divide if there is any escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peo-ple is a bad division; Cae-sar is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules for derivatives from words ending in consonant where accent shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in certain letters, in divisions, the consonant should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative has retained the accent of the parent-word, leave the consonant in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); deject-ive (from deject').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s adding syllable does not justify new division
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s, adding a new syllable to words ending in an s-sound, does not create an excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "horses" and "circumstan-ces" are impossible divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide adjectives in -cal on the -ic syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the / (the -ic): physi-cal, not phys-ical or physic-al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Rule 230, admonition: do not split the word.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use superior figures for reference indices in text; place after punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule, use superior figures. Index figures in the text should be placed after the punctuation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ...which were then invading Attic prose,1 and which made ...; footnote example markers shown. Use asterisk/dagger only in special cases like tabular or algebraic matter (see 233).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence for non-figure footnote marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When figures are not used, the sequence of indices should be: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'ibid.' for immediately repeated references; limit its use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use ibid. instead of repeating the title. This ibid. takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ibid. should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso page; better to repeat title if short, or use loc. cit. or op. cit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote formatting for tables: size and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether the tables are ruled or open, should be in 6-pt., and should invariably be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page. For reference indices in such cases use asterisks, etc., and not superior figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: If author's name appears in text, omit it from footnote
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to, or a quotation from, his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided showing in-text attribution followed by footnote giving title/location only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place index figure after a quotation rather than before
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text after the quotation than before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See illustration earlier in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit abbreviations Vol./chap./p. ordinarily; use numeral conventions for classical refs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, omit "Vol.", "chap.", and "p." in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division, except in reference to ancient/classical authors when lower-case roman numerals should be used; Roman numerals (lower-case) for chapter and pages of introductory matter; Arabic numerals for number (leaf) and text pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use Vol./p. etc. when confusion would arise. In classical references use periods instead of commas; in English references the classical convention may be followed if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place date in periodical references immediately after volume number in parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number, and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration shown earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number footnotes consecutively through an article/chapter in linotype work
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article, in a journal, or through a chapter, in a book, to save resetting in case of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Exceptions exist for certain journals (Botanical Gazette, Astrophysical Journal, Classical Philology, Classical Journal) which adopt different styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: list French/Belgian/Spanish names under prefix in certain cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In indexes and other alphabetical lists of names, a French, Belgian, or Spanish name preceded by "le," "la," "l'", "du," or "des" should be listed under the letters of the prefix in advance of the ordinary "L" or "D" list; if preceded by "de" or "d'", under the first letter of the word following the prefix, with the particle placed after initials or Christian name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Conte, John; La Noue, François de; L'Estrange, Sir Roger; Du Maurier, George. Note: if the particle is actually part of the surname, index under the particle (De Bey, De Quincey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: German 'von' names under following name; Mac/Mc rules
rubrics_metrics.description: German names preceded by "von" should be indexed according to the initials of the name following the prefix. Names beginning with "M'", "Mac", or "Mc" with the following letter capitalized should be indexed in advance of the ordinary "M" list, arranged alphabetically by letters following the prefix; names beginning with "Mac" without capitalization take their ordinary M-place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sternthal, Max von; Goethe, J. W. von.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: O'/St./Van capitalization rules and 'and'/'&'/'y'/'et' handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Names preceded by "O'", "St.", or "Van", with the following letter capitalized, should be placed in advance of the "O", "S", or "V" list and arranged alphabetically according to the letter following the prefix. Names with two parts or firms connected by "and", "&", "y" (Spanish), or "et" (French) should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith and Evans under S; Gomez y Pineda under G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: hyphenated names listed by following name if English, preceding if French
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated names should be listed according to the name following the hyphen, if English; according to the name preceding the hyphen, if French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Taylor, Henry Chandler- (for Henry Chandler-Taylor); Saint-Saens, Charles Camille (for Charles Camille Saint Saëns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular type sizes based on body type size
rubrics_metrics.description: In 12-pt. and 10-pt. matter open (unruled) tables should ordinarily be set in 9-pt. leaded; ruled, in 8-pt. solid. In 9-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt. matter open tables in 6-pt. leaded; ruled, 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled tables set in 6-pt. solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 240 prescribes sizing conventions for tables relative to body type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions/box-heads sizing and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables where box-heads have several stories, upper (primary) heads set in caps and small caps; lower (secondary) in caps and lower-case. Stubs usually also in caps and small caps when small caps used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 241.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between table rules and matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en-quad between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 242.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders use in open and ruled tables; leaders between columns of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables set by hand, periods one em apart and aligned should be used between columns; when set on the linotype machine, use regular leaders. In ruled tables, in the stub, leaders should usually be employed if there is room. In columns of figures, for blanks use leaders the width of the largest number in the column; center the figures in the column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 243–244: leaders are period or hyphen leaders; for four-digit numbers use 2-em leader, etc.; if figures cannot be exactly centered and digit groups unequal, leave more space on the left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter in table columns centered; use hanging indentation for overflow
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention, and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 245.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set tables and columns to even picas/nonpareils when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: All tables, and the individual columns in tables, should be set to even picas, or nonpareils, if practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 246.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules at top of tables; two-column tables open, three+ ruled
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but perpendicular double rules only when a table is doubled up on itself. Tables of two columns only should be set as open; of three or more, as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules 247 and 248.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering/headline typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Table I," etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following descriptive line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single descriptive headline not preceded by the table number should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 249.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point is the typographical unit; pica is standard measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica (12 points = one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show lines set in 12-pt (pica), 11-pt (small pica), 10-pt (long primer), 9-pt (bourgeois), 8-pt (brevier), 7-pt (minion), 6-pt (nonpareil), 5-pt (pearl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of basic type styles and manuscript indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman. Type with a sloping face is called italic; italic is indicated in manuscripts by a straight line under the words. Type with a heavy black face is called bold-face; indicated by a wavy line in manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative sample lines set in roman, italics, bold-face are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of type and font composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of a type is called the shank; the upper surface bearing the character is the face; the projecting part of the face is the kern; the projecting part of the shank is the shoulder. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript marks: caps indicated by three straight lines, small caps by two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of quads, em-, en-spaces and dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: An em-quad (em) is a square block equal to the current point size; an en-quad is half an em in width. An em-dash is the width of an em; an en-dash the width of an en-quad. Three-em, two-em, and other em dashes described. Hair-space is thinner than a 5-em.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of lines spaced with various quads/spaces, and display of dashes and en-dashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard interword and punctuation spacing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation points than commas, and after commas; an en-quad after semicolons, and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em-quad after periods, and exclamation and interrogation points concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary to reduce spacing, begin with commas and slanted letters; if increasing, begin with overlapping letters and straight letters, then points other than periods and commas. Maintain proportion: majority of words at 3-em space, the rest at most en-quad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternating extreme spacing; do not hair-space to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, if avoidable. Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of paragraph or allow end indention
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 267.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short words should have equal spacing each side
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like "a", "an," etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 268.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thin space after §, ¶, and before 'f.'/'ff.' and metric symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, ¶, and similar signs; before "f.", "ff.", and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "§ 14. Be it further ordained ..."; pp. 10 ff.; 16 cm.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between currency symbols and numerals in American/English sums
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols ($, £, s., d.) and the numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $2.75; £10 7s. 2d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at start of lines and caps/headings spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic numerals at the beginning of lines denoting subsections there should be an en-quad; after Roman numerals, an em-quad. After Roman numerals in cap/cap-and-small-cap/small-cap center-heads there should be an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 271.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture references spacing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 272.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insert spaces between letters in products or before super/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A1 v' = 2m^(v^2 — 2vwyz + 2'w^y').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation amounts by measure and point size
rubrics_metrics.description: In measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of 10–20 picas, indent amounts vary by point size (11-pt, 10-pt, 9-pt, 8-pt = 1½ ems; 6-pt = 2 ems). In measures of 20–30 picas, indent amounts increase (specific chart provided). These are for plain paragraphs; hanging indention rules differ with measure and point size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 274 gives specific indent values for plain and hanging indentions by measure and point size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation: center longest line; govern indentation by rhymes and line length
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let indent govern by that. If longest line disproportionately long, use an average. When quotations from different poems vary slightly, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines; align blank verse approximately. For consecutive rhyming lines align or indent according to rhyme pattern; indent disproportionately short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 275 with illustrative poetic excerpts and guidance for rhyme alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain paragraphs; use hanging indention to emphasize opening words or numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter plain paragraphs are always preferable. Use hanging indention when desired to bring into relief the opening word(s) of a paragraph, the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 284 for hanging indention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and standard sizes of leads and slugs
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads is called leaded; without, solid. A slug is a thicker strip used in make-up; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points (nonpareil and pica) thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules 277–278: nearly all books are leaded; examples given of leaded vs solid paragraphs.
